decks.title: Opening the conversation
decks.blurb: Agree how you’ll talk before anything hard comes up.
decks.why: Most families don’t struggle with the topics. They struggle with how to talk about them. Start here to agree the ground rules together.

questions.text: Why did each of us agree to sit down for this today?
questions.tip: Go around the table. Short answers are fine.

questions.text: What’s one thing you hope we’ll understand better by the end?
questions.tip: Remember these. You can check in on them at the end.

questions.text: What makes talking about money or health hard in our family?
questions.tip: Name the feeling, not the person. “It feels awkward” works better than “You never…”

questions.text: Did your family talk about these things when you were growing up? What was that like?
questions.tip: Parents first. Their answer often explains a lot.

questions.text: What would make this conversation feel safe for you?
questions.tip: Listen for simple asks, like no phones or no interrupting, and agree to them.

questions.text: Is there anything you’d rather not talk about today?
questions.tip: Respect every answer. Skip those cards when they come up.

questions.text: How should we handle it if we disagree?
questions.tip: Try agreeing on a pause word anyone can say to take a break.

questions.text: Who else should eventually be part of these conversations?
questions.tip: Think siblings, partners or a trusted advisor.

questions.text: How often should we come back to these talks?
questions.tip: Tie it to a moment you already share, like a holiday or birthday.

questions.text: What’s a worry you’ve been carrying that you haven’t said out loud?
questions.tip: Just listen. You don’t need to solve it today.

decks.title: What matters most
decks.blurb: The values and hopes behind every other decision.
decks.why: Values are the anchor. Every later decision, from care to inheritance, comes back to what matters most to each of you.

questions.text: What does a good life look like to you right now?
questions.tip: There’s no right answer. Let each person finish before anyone responds.

questions.text: What are you most proud of in how our family gets through hard times?
questions.tip: Share a specific moment, not a general trait.

questions.text: What has money made possible for you, and what has it never fixed?
questions.tip: Both halves matter. Take turns on each.

questions.text: What values do you hope our family carries forward?
questions.tip: Name one value each, then see where you overlap.

questions.text: What do you want the next ten years to feel like?
questions.tip: Kids: ask one follow-up question before sharing your own view.

questions.text: What does “being secure” mean to you?
questions.tip: Notice where answers differ. That’s useful, not a problem.

questions.text: How do you think each generation in our family sees money differently?
questions.tip: Each person explains their own view, not someone else’s.

questions.text: What would you want us to do differently from how you did it?
questions.tip: Kids: say thank you. This one takes honesty.

questions.text: What do you hope we never have to worry about?
questions.tip: Kids: ask why this one feels important to them.

questions.text: What worries you most about our family’s future?
questions.tip: Acknowledge each worry before moving on.

decks.title: Everyday money
decks.blurb: Who handles the bills, and what happens if they can’t.
decks.why: The most common money crisis isn’t inheritance. It’s the day one parent can’t pay the bills and nobody else knows how.

questions.text: Who handles the bills and day-to-day money in your house?
questions.tip: Start simple. Who, not how much.

questions.text: How did you decide who does what with money?
questions.tip: Often it just happened. That’s a fine answer.

questions.text: Who would you call first with a money question?
questions.tip: Kids answer too. It’s useful to hear everyone’s go-to person.

questions.text: If the person who handles the money couldn’t for a month, what would happen?
questions.tip: Walk through it like a practice run, step by step.

questions.text: Does more than one person know how to get into the accounts?
questions.tip: No passwords needed. Just whether someone else could.

questions.text: Which bills are automatic, and which need someone to pay them?
questions.tip: A rough list is enough. Details can come later.

questions.text: Have you had any scam calls or suspicious messages lately? What did you do?
questions.tip: Share your own close calls too. Everyone gets them.

questions.text: Is managing money getting harder, easier or about the same?
questions.tip: Keep it light. This isn’t a test.

questions.text: What help with money, if any, would you welcome from us?
questions.tip: Kids: offer, don’t insist.

questions.text: If we noticed you were struggling with bills, what would you want us to do?
questions.tip: Agree on what you’d do now, so no one has to guess later.

decks.title: Will you be okay?
decks.blurb: Confidence about the years ahead, without sharing numbers.
decks.why: Adult children’s biggest worry is whether their parents’ money will last. These questions ask about plans and confidence, never balances.

questions.text: What does a typical week in retirement look like, or how do you picture it?
questions.tip: Make it specific: mornings, people, places.

questions.text: What surprised you most about retiring, or about planning for it?
questions.tip: Kids: ask what they wish they’d known sooner.

questions.text: Where will your income come from once you stop working?
questions.tip: Name the sources only. No amounts needed.

questions.text: Has anyone, like an advisor, reviewed your plan with you?
questions.tip: If no one has, that’s useful to know, not a failure.

questions.text: If costs keep rising, what would you change first?
questions.tip: Treat it as a what-if, not a prediction.

questions.text: How confident are you that your money will last as long as you need it?
questions.tip: A simple scale works: very, somewhat or not sure.

questions.text: If one of you lived much longer than the other, would the other be okay?
questions.tip: This can feel heavy. Go slowly.

questions.text: Would you tell us if money got tight? What would make that easier to say?
questions.tip: Kids: say what you’d want to hear in return.

questions.text: Is anyone at this table counting on help from the others, now or later?
questions.tip: Help goes both ways, from parents to kids and kids to parents.

questions.text: What would “being okay” look like for each of us twenty years from now?
questions.tip: Everyone answers for themselves, not for each other.

decks.title: Health and medical wishes
decks.blurb: Who decides, and what matters, if health changes.
decks.why: The hardest family decisions are often medical, made in a hospital hallway. Talking now means no one has to guess later.

questions.text: What does a good day look like for you, even if your health changes?
questions.tip: Small details matter, like a morning walk or a phone call.

questions.text: Who supports you most when things get hard?
questions.tip: Use names, not roles. Who do you actually call?

questions.text: If you were very sick, would you want to know everything or just the basics?
questions.tip: There’s no right answer, and it can be different for each of you.

questions.text: If you couldn’t speak for yourself, who would you want making medical decisions?
questions.tip: Name a first choice and a backup.

questions.text: Does that person know, and is it written down?
questions.tip: If not, a healthcare proxy form makes it official. A doctor can explain how.

questions.text: Who should, and shouldn’t, be told about your health?
questions.tip: Think about who should hear news first.

questions.text: Are there treatments you’d want to avoid, even if they might extend your life?
questions.tip: Describe what you’d want life to look like, not only treatments.

questions.text: At what point would you want care to focus on comfort rather than cure?
questions.tip: This is a hard one. “I’m not sure yet” is a fine answer.

questions.text: Is there a future moment you very much want to be there for?
questions.tip: Let this be a warm one. Share what you’re looking forward to.

questions.text: Should we follow your wishes exactly, or do what gives us peace?
questions.tip: Kids: listen first. This answer is a gift.

decks.title: Care and living later
decks.blurb: Where to live and who helps, before it’s urgent.
decks.why: Care is where money, family roles and independence meet. Talking early keeps it a choice instead of an emergency.

questions.text: What do you love most about where you live now?
questions.tip: Starting here makes later questions feel less like a threat.

questions.text: Where do you see yourselves living in ten years?
questions.tip: Dreams are welcome, not just plans.

questions.text: If stairs or driving became hard, what would you want to do?
questions.tip: Talk about changes that would help, not only moving.

questions.text: If you needed help at home, who would you want helping?
questions.tip: Name both family and paid help.

questions.text: How would long-term care be paid for if you needed it?
questions.tip: If it hasn’t been planned, that’s a good next step, not a failure.

questions.text: What can each of us realistically offer, given our jobs and families?
questions.tip: Be honest about time and distance. It prevents resentment later.

questions.text: How would you feel about moving closer to one of us, or living together?
questions.tip: Everyone can feel differently. Hear all the answers first.

questions.text: What would you never want to happen if you needed care?
questions.tip: Kids: take this seriously. It guides decisions later.

questions.text: How should we share the work of caring for you if it comes to that?
questions.tip: Talk about who’s nearby and who could help from afar.

questions.text: What would make accepting help feel okay to you?
questions.tip: Kids: ask what kind of help feels respectful.

decks.title: Wills and important documents
decks.blurb: What exists, where it is and who to call.
decks.why: You don’t need to read the documents. You only need to know they exist, where they are and who to call.

questions.text: Have any of your friends had to sort things out for a parent? What did they wish they’d known?
questions.tip: Stories make this easier. Start with someone else’s.

questions.text: Do you have a will or a trust? When was it last updated?
questions.tip: Yes, no and not sure are all fine answers.

questions.text: Is someone named to handle your money if you couldn’t?
questions.tip: This is often called a financial power of attorney.

questions.text: Are the beneficiaries on your accounts and insurance still who you’d choose?
questions.tip: Marriages, divorces and births are good reasons to check.

questions.text: If we needed your important papers tomorrow, where would we look?
questions.tip: A place is enough. You don’t need to look now.

questions.text: Who helped you with these documents, and would they talk to us if needed?
questions.tip: A name and how to reach them is all you need.

questions.text: How do you keep track of passwords and online accounts?
questions.tip: Where they’re kept, never the passwords themselves.

questions.text: Is there anything you’ve been meaning to put in writing?
questions.tip: Kids: offer to help book an appointment.

questions.text: Have we kids made our own wills, or named anyone for our children?
questions.tip: Kids answer this one. It keeps things fair.

questions.text: What’s gotten in the way of finishing any of this?
questions.tip: Common answers: time, cost, not knowing where to start.

decks.title: Inheritance and fairness
decks.blurb: What “fair” means to each of you.
decks.why: Families rarely fall out over how much is left. They fall out over surprises and what feels unfair. Talking now prevents both.

questions.text: What did you inherit from your parents, in money, things or lessons?
questions.tip: Lessons count as much as money or things.

questions.text: How was inheritance handled in your family growing up, and how did it feel?
questions.tip: Listen for what felt fair or unfair to them.

questions.text: Is there anything, like the house or a keepsake, you’d want to stay in the family?
questions.tip: Name the thing and why it matters.

questions.text: Would you rather help us now, while you can see it, or later?
questions.tip: There’s no right answer. Each choice has trade-offs.

questions.text: Does “fair” mean “equal” to you?
questions.tip: Expect different answers. That’s the point of asking.

questions.text: How would you handle it if one of us has needed more help than the others?
questions.tip: Kids: try not to defend or keep score.

questions.text: How much do you want us to know about your plans, and when?
questions.tip: Parents decide this. Kids: respect the answer.

questions.text: Do any of us feel we’re expected to count on an inheritance, or not to?
questions.tip: Be honest about what you’ve assumed.

questions.text: What would you want us to know how to do before anything is passed on?
questions.tip: Think skills, not amounts: managing money, knowing who to call.

questions.text: What would you hope we never argue about?
questions.tip: End on agreement. Say the shared answer out loud.

decks.title: Who does what
decks.blurb: Executor, caregiver and who keeps everyone in the loop.
decks.why: Many parents have already picked someone for these roles without telling them. Saying it out loud avoids resentment later.

questions.text: Who in our family is the organizer, and who is the peacemaker?
questions.tip: Keep it playful. Everyone has a role.

questions.text: If something happened, who would you want sorting out your affairs?
questions.tip: This person is usually called the executor.

questions.text: Does that person know, and are they willing?
questions.tip: If they’re at the table, ask them directly.

questions.text: If you needed care, who would you hope would coordinate it?
questions.tip: It doesn’t have to be the same person as the executor.

questions.text: Is there anything you’d want one of us to learn how to do now, just in case?
questions.tip: Pick one small thing to show them soon.

questions.text: How should we keep everyone in the loop, including those who live far away?
questions.tip: Agree on a way, like a group chat or a monthly call.

questions.text: What would you not want any of us involved in?
questions.tip: Kids: hear this as a boundary, not a rejection.

questions.text: How do we make sure one person doesn’t end up carrying everything?
questions.tip: Be honest about what’s realistic for you.

questions.text: How should we decide together when we disagree?
questions.tip: Agree on a tiebreaker now, while it’s calm.

questions.text: How can we help without it feeling like we’re taking over?
questions.tip: Parents: give one example of help that feels good.

decks.title: End of life and legacy
decks.blurb: How you want to be remembered, and your final wishes.
decks.why: Legacy is what people most want to talk about once they start. These are the hardest questions, so take them slowly.

questions.text: What do you hope people remember about you?
questions.tip: Ask for the story behind the answer.

questions.text: What stories do you want your grandchildren to know?
questions.tip: Ask for one story now. Others can come later.

questions.text: Is there a belonging you’d want a specific person to have?
questions.tip: Saying it out loud now can prevent hurt feelings later.

questions.text: Are there causes or people outside the family you’d want to support?
questions.tip: This can include friends, places of worship or charities.

questions.text: Do you have wishes for a funeral or memorial?
questions.tip: Small details count: music, place, who speaks.

questions.text: If you could choose, where would you want to be at the end of your life?
questions.tip: Home, hospital or somewhere else. It’s okay to be unsure.

questions.text: Who would you want with you?
questions.tip: Go gently. Pause if anyone needs a moment.

questions.text: Is there something you’d want to say to someone that you haven’t yet?
questions.tip: You don’t have to say it here. Naming it is enough.

questions.text: Would you like to write a letter or record a message for the family?
questions.tip: Kids: offer to help them get started.

questions.text: How would you like us to remember you on hard days, like anniversaries?
questions.tip: End with something warm. Say thank you to each other.
